passageEn: Marta owns a small shop in the center of town. She wakes up at four every morning to start making bread before the shop opens. Her shop opens at seven and closes at two in the afternoon, six days a week. On Sundays she stays home and rests. Marta learned to make bread from her grandmother, who taught her to work by hand instead of using machines. Many customers say her bread tastes better than bread from the market. Last year, Marta hired her first worker, a young man named Daniel, to help her prepare orders for local restaurants. Marta hopes to open a second shop in another town within the next two years.

passageEn:
In the early 2000s, marine biologists began noticing that large sections of coral reefs around the world were turning pale and losing their vivid colors within just a few weeks. This process, known as coral bleaching, alarmed scientists because healthy reefs support an enormous variety of fish and other sea creatures that depend on the coral for food and shelter.
The most widely accepted explanation is that bleaching happens when ocean temperatures rise even slightly above normal. Coral polyps host tiny algae inside their tissue, and these algae both feed the coral and give it its bright color. When water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae, leaving behind a pale, stressed structure that struggles to survive without its usual food source.
However, several recent studies have complicated this simple picture. Some reefs exposed to unusually warm water for weeks did not bleach at all, while nearby reefs in cooler water bleached severely. Researchers now suspect that factors such as water pollution, local currents, and even the specific type of algae present may influence how a given reef responds to heat, meaning temperature alone cannot fully explain why one reef survives and another does not.
